ranked_candidates.hidden_signal_to_verify: Foodservice and restaurant revenue mix, customer concentration, utilization of extract and ready-to-drink capacity, new-program wins with chain operators, debt burden, commodity pass-through, and whether scale is improving margins.
ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need company filings or earnings-call disclosure that separates foodservice, restaurant, convenience-store, retail, and CPG exposure; also need evidence that Conway utilization and new beverage contracts translate into margin expansion rather than only revenue growth.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Highest-priority Serenity candidate in this chunk. The company appears to sit one step behind restaurant and foodservice beverage menus as a scaled outsourced coffee, tea, extract, RTD, and private-label beverage platform. External evidence describes Westrock as a one-stop-shop beverage partner with broad blue-chip customers, a large Conway bottling/canning facility, extract-based beverage capabilities, and recent 5-year contracts with Starbucks and Monster Energy. That creates a clearer chokepoint thesis than a simple commodity coffee story: customers may outsource formulation, roasting, extraction, packaging, freight simplification, and traceability to a specialized scaled supplier.
ranked_candidates.why_underfollowed: Often screened as coffee, consumer staples, or commodity-sensitive beverage manufacturing rather than as restaurant, convenience-store, and foodservice infrastructure. The hidden signal is not restaurant traffic itself but whether foodservice chains and beverage brands are outsourcing more beverage complexity to Westrock's vertically integrated platform.

ranked_candidates.hidden_signal_to_verify: Supply-chain revenue and margin mix, franchisee purchase requirements, profit-sharing structure, food inflation pass-through, supply-center throughput, franchisee unit economics, and erosion or reinforcement of first-party ordering after aggregator partnerships.
ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: For this Layer 3 funnel, the evidence gap is not whether Domino's has a strong model; it is whether its model helps identify smaller public companies with similar supply-chain control but lower market attention.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Domino's scores extremely well as a reference model for the theme because it demonstrates how restaurant value can accrue to captive procurement, dough manufacturing, franchisee ordering requirements, delivery logistics, and first-party digital demand rather than just restaurant-level sales. External and cached evidence cite vertically integrated dough manufacturing and food distribution centers, required franchisee purchasing, procurement scale, loyalty members, and direct ordering rails. However, it is not ranked above underfollowed candidates for research priority because the task prioritizes hidden supply-chain discovery, and DPZ is a widely followed large-cap restaurant operator.
ranked_candidates.why_underfollowed: Not underfollowed as a stock. It is included only as a reference anchor for finding less obvious companies that replicate parts of its procurement, distribution, supply-chain, and digital-ordering economics.

ranked_candidates.hidden_signal_to_verify: Organic case growth, customer retention, independent restaurant health, acquisition integration, distribution-center density, gross margin stability, and sensitivity to freight and commodity inflation.
ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need current filing and earnings-call evidence on organic growth versus acquisition-driven growth, exposure by customer type, and whether gross-margin stability reflects real sourcing power or temporary pricing benefits.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Strong underfollowed infrastructure candidate because specialty distribution maps directly to restaurant procurement complexity, premium ingredients, independent restaurant health, and route-density economics. Compared with broadline distribution, CHEF has a more differentiated specialty-food angle and a purer restaurant-demand read-through. Its thesis is also highly falsifiable through case growth, organic sales, margin stability, acquisition integration, and customer retention.
ranked_candidates.why_underfollowed: Specialty food distribution receives less attention than restaurant brands, delivery marketplaces, or mega-cap broadline distributors. It may be missed by restaurant-theme screens because it is categorized as distribution rather than a restaurant operating model.

ranked_candidates.hidden_signal_to_verify: Foodservice segment case volume, independent restaurant growth, chain-account wins, custom protein processing contribution, distribution-center utilization, leverage, M&A integration, and margin sensitivity to food inflation.
ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need segment-level evidence that restaurant and foodservice demand, rather than acquisitions or inflation pass-through alone, is driving durable volume and margin improvement.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: Solid but less differentiated restaurant-infrastructure candidate. PFGC has direct exposure to foodservice distribution, procurement outsourcing, route density, independent restaurant volumes, chain accounts, and custom protein processing. It is relevant to the theme because foodservice distribution can be a scaling layer for restaurants that cannot replicate captive procurement systems like Domino's. It ranks below WEST and CHEF because it is larger, less obscure, and likely has more investor coverage.
ranked_candidates.why_underfollowed: Not obscure by size, but its role as restaurant infrastructure may be overlooked because distribution is often viewed as low-margin and operationally mundane rather than as a procurement, logistics, and route-density bottleneck.

ranked_candidates.hidden_signal_to_verify: Liquidity, customer concentration, route density, gross margin stability, coffee pounds shipped, sustainability of direct-store-delivery base after the Northlake sale, debt profile, and whether disclosed restaurant-chain relationships are current and material.
ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need proof that the remaining DSD base is stable, profitable, and restaurant-relevant after the Northlake sale and direct-ship customer changes. Also need balance-sheet and liquidity verification before treating the hidden signal as investable research quality.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: FARM has a direct but fragile restaurant and foodservice beverage signal. External evidence describes Farmer Brothers as a nationwide coffee roaster, wholesaler, and service provider with customers including restaurants, convenience stores, hotels, coffee shops, and hospitals; it also emphasizes a DSD-focused business, a single SQF-certified Portland roasting facility, and a streamlined post-Northlake operating model. It is highly underfollowed and falsifiable, but its micro-cap status and operational turnaround risk prevent a higher research ranking.
ranked_candidates.why_underfollowed: Extremely small, operationally challenged, and hidden behind customer beverage programs. It may be missed by restaurant screens despite recurring foodservice exposure because the company looks like a distressed coffee distributor rather than a restaurant-demand derivative.

ranked_candidates.hidden_signal_to_verify: Whether TreeHouse has meaningful current revenue from QSRs, restaurant chains, foodservice distributors, convenience stores, or approved-vendor contracts rather than mostly retail grocery private label.
ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need direct disclosure of current restaurant, QSR, foodservice, distributor, or convenience-store customer exposure. Without that, the thesis remains an inference from manufacturing capability rather than a proven restaurant-infrastructure position.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: TreeHouse remains worth tracking because the restaurant angle could be hidden inside private-label manufacturing, coffee assets, and foodservice or convenience-store relationships. Its underfollowed score is high because it is usually framed as retail private label rather than restaurant supply-chain infrastructure. However, the current evidence quality is weaker than for WEST or CHEF because the restaurant and foodservice revenue connection remains unverified.
ranked_candidates.why_underfollowed: Usually categorized as a private-label packaged-food company rather than a restaurant or foodservice procurement beneficiary. Any restaurant exposure may be embedded inside acquired coffee and manufacturing assets rather than obvious from headline segment labels.

ranked_candidates.hidden_signal_to_verify: Foodservice versus retail mix, distributor concentration, chain-restaurant customers, franchise-approved vendor status, durable menu-component dependency, capacity constraints, liquidity, governance, and whether any major restaurant chains rely on its products.
ranked_candidates.main_evidence_gap: Need primary-source disclosure or credible channel evidence showing material foodservice or chain-restaurant revenue. Without that, the restaurant-supplier thesis remains speculation.
ranked_candidates.why_prioritized: AMNF is the most speculative shadow candidate in the chunk. It fits the Serenity underfollowed lens because menu-component suppliers can be overlooked if their products flow through distributors or private-label channels into restaurants. However, the current evidence is too thin to rank higher: restaurant exposure, customer concentration, approved-vendor status, and foodservice mix are not yet proven.
ranked_candidates.why_underfollowed: OTC micro-cap profile, narrow product category, limited disclosure, and indirect restaurant exposure make it easy to miss in a restaurant-theme screen.

summary: Split Layer 3 ranking merged from candidate chunks.
